## One commit after the audit: `17f19df` fixes a claim this branch documents but did not honor

The completion audit ran the whole plan checklist against the tree rather than against this description, and one item did not hold. `ARCHITECTURE.md` 6.5 and `internal/sep1/guard.go` both say a `home_domain` of only whitespace is an absent domain that must not become a fetch. The fixtures corpus says that shape is real mainnet data: `whitespace-home-domain` is a public-network read whose field is a single space, and its own scenario line is "home_domain is a single space, which a tool that trims before validating reads as absent".

Three places asked the question as a comparison with the empty string instead, so none of them trimmed:

- `internal/run/run.go` decided a fetch was worth making, `sep1` refused `" "` at the hostname step, and `id-toml-unreachable` printed a WARN about an unverified identity claim for an account that publishes nothing.
- `internal/rules/identity.go` failed the opposite way twice: `id-no-home-domain` stayed silent when the policy declared a domain and the chain showed a space, and the toml rules would speak from any result left in the context regardless of the field.

The question now has one answer, `model.AccountSnapshot.HasHomeDomain`, and the run's fetch decision plus all three identity suppressions ask it. Blank is absent; invalid is still not. A padded but real domain is still fetched, and a non-ASCII host is still refused at the guard and reported as unreachable, so the two behaviors this branch already documents are untouched.

Tests were written first and seen failing on the pre-fix tree, which is the evidence the defect was reachable rather than theoretical:

- `TestABlankObservedDomainIsNoDomain` emitted `id-toml-unreachable` with evidence `step not-attempted; home domain` (and, for the stale-result case, `step hostname`).
- `TestRunTreatsABlankObservedDomainAsAbsent` recorded an identity fetch of `" "` and of `"\t"`, while the padded-real-domain case passed before and after.
- `TestAccountSnapshotHasHomeDomain` is the table for the predicate itself.

`AGENTS.md` section 5 re-run on `17f19df`: `gofmt -l .` empty, `go vet ./...` clean, `staticcheck 2026.2.2 (0.8.2)` silent, `go test ./... -race -count=1` all packages ok, `grep -rn "net/http" internal/rules/ internal/model/` empty, and the four roadmap scripts green. No gate in this branch changed behavior, and nothing about the SSRF Done-when moved: the guard tests are untouched.

Docs updated to match, in the same commit as the behavior: `PRD.md` 6.1, `ARCHITECTURE.md` 6.5, 6.7 and 9, and `ROADMAP.md` carries it in 3.5's note plus a changelog row, said plainly as an audit finding rather than a bug report.

Still untested, unchanged from the description above: nothing in this branch has fetched a real `stellar.toml`, there is no live DNS rebinding attacker, and the hop cap is untested against a server that ignores it. The three owner questions stand.

Task 1.9 was ticked 2026-10-28 and this issue stayed open by accident.

Closed by `b608e13`, the merge of PR #107 on 2026-11-03: `internal/sep1` went from a package stub to a `guard.go`, `fetch.go` and `parse.go` that fetch a `stellar.toml` through a dial-time address guard, and `internal/rules` registered `id-no-home-domain`, `id-toml-unreachable` and `id-toml-account-unlisted` on top of it. Seven of sixteen rules are live and a run can fail on an identity claim.

Two things it left as the task line says plainly: no test in the tree dials a real domain, and `PRD.md` 6.1's `NETWORK_PASSPHRASE` sentence has no rule ID behind it yet. The value is carried as a fact for 3.7 and compared by nothing.

Corrected 2026-11-03 after this comment was written. The first clause above said the fetcher had never read a real domain; at 15:05Z the same afternoon it did, against a live testnet issuer: account `GDSX2WUFUT7KCMTUNG3IUQWIUQSC4XNKQ5NTGEZRKLTMLCSJTCUVBEVG`, home domain `komunitin.org`, which answered HTTP 200 with an HTML body, so the strict parse refused it and the run reported `id-toml-unreachable` at WARN and exited 1 under `--fail-on warn`. That is the designed behavior on a real third-party answer rather than a simulated one. The command and its transcript are in `docs/RECORDING.md`, in the docs pull request that follows this one. What still holds: no test in the tree dials a real domain, the address classes the guard refuses are proven by tests and not by runs, and the redirect hop cap has never been pointed at a server that ignores it.

Closed by #111 (merge `eb9b94f`, 2026-11-04), which ticked `ROADMAP.md` task 0.7.

The task is answered, but not by the method its title names. Every question it asks is a deterministic rule the network enforces in public, version-stable code, and producing the states by hand means submitting a transaction, which `AGENTS.md` section 4 forbids this project. So the four answers were read from the implementation instead: `stellar/stellar-core` v30.0.0 at `0e49751aa9ddf892302cca02cea7f3f5d97df9f1` (the build `testdata/horizon/root-testnet.json` names in `core_version`) and re-read at v29.0.0 `a9d72b0cac3a89ebbcf926af449ac73089e0f8f7`, so no answer rests on which protocol version happens to be active, with the XDR from `stellar/stellar-xdr` v30.0.

- A threshold-0 account with a weight-0 master and no other signer authorizes nothing: `TransactionFrame.cpp:428-444` leaves the master out under `if (acc.thresholds[0])` and `SignatureChecker.cpp:89-118` reaches the weight comparison only from inside a signature match, so an empty candidate list returns false.
- Leftover signatures invalidate the transaction: `SignatureChecker.cpp:171-191` into `txBAD_AUTH_EXTRA` at `TransactionFrame.cpp:1571-1575`.
- An unreachable or out-of-order tier is a state the ledger stores: `SetOptionsOpFrame.cpp:230-328` validates ranges and the not-master key only, and `SetOptionsResultCode` has no code for an unreachable threshold.
- `hash(x)` is a hash lock, not a signature: `SignatureUtils.cpp:83-91` compares `signerKey.hashX()` to `sha256(sig.signature)`, hint from the last four bytes at `:107-124`.

Two of the four answers were corrections rather than confirmations, and both became work: the participating set is four key types (`Stellar-types.x:47-53`), which `internal/model/signer.go` did not carry, filed as task 2.11 and closed by #112; and reachability is capped at the 20 signature slots an envelope holds against an account that can hold 20 entries plus a nonzero master, which 2.3 implements and #113 closed.

What is *not* claimed by closing this: any observation. No account Gauge has read exhibits a zero-weight master with no other signer, an unused signature, an unreachable tier or a `hash(x)` entry. The semantics are verified; the fixtures still are not, and that is task 3.6, whose issue is #42.

`ARCHITECTURE.md` 6.3 and 15, `ARCHITECTURE_ESSENTIALS.md` 7 and 14 and `PRD.md` 2.1, 12 and 14 were rewritten from those citations, which retired the `[Unverified]` marker 6.3 had carried since 0.1.

Closed: task 0.7 is ticked on main at eb9b94f (PR #111). The four semantics were verified from the protocol implementation rather than a testnet submission, for the reason given in the comment above, and the two corrections that reading produced are closed too: 2.11 by #112 and 2.3 by #113.

Closed by #113 (merge `7805608`, 2026-11-04), which ticked `ROADMAP.md` task 2.3.

`internal/threshold` exports `Reachable` and `MinSigners` over one shared participating-weights list, so the 20-signature cap cannot be applied in one function and forgotten in the other. The list drops entries at weight 0, because `TransactionFrame::checkSignature` leaves a zero-weight master out of the candidates and `SetOptionsOpFrame` treats any other zero weight as a delete; drops every `T...` entry, because a pre-authorized transaction hash is bound to one transaction and is not standing control; sorts the survivors descending; and truncates to 20, because an envelope carries `DecoratedSignature signatures<20>` while an account can hold `MAX_SIGNERS = 20` entries plus a nonzero master. Threshold 0 answers true only when at least one candidate exists, the rule 0.7 pulled from `SignatureChecker.cpp:89-118` and `:168`.

Testing, which is the part this issue asked for: sixteen named table cases and 5000 randomized draws of up to 10 signers across all four key types, compared against subset enumeration. That cross-check is the test of the greedy claim that largest-first minimizes the count. The random sets stay under 20 because a subset search over 21 is the exponential case the cap exists to avoid, so the cap carries named cases instead. Three mutations were run to prove the tests bite: dropping the `T...` exclusion, dropping the truncation, and dropping the empty-candidate rule each failed a named case and the comparison.

One acceptance line was amended rather than lowered. FR-04 read "fixtures captured from real accounts and testnet experiments (task 0.7)"; 0.7 closed by reading the implementation, so the criterion now names the verified semantics and the brute-force cross-check and leaves the observed-account half to 3.6, where it can actually be met. That half is #42.

`internal/threshold` is a pure package: no I/O, no time, no randomness outside test code. It became the second socket-free reason a signer rule can be written at all, and 3.1 (#37) is the consumer that landed on it nine rules deep.
Task 2.3 is ticked on main at 7805608 (PR #113). Phase 2 is 11 of 11 on that merge.

Closed by #114 (merge `c7931d7`, 2026-11-04), which ticked `ROADMAP.md` task 3.1.

All nine rules register: six in `internal/rules/signers.go` and three in `internal/rules/thresholds.go`, in catalog order between the account rules and the flag rules, so a run evaluates sixteen rather than seven. Each one calls `internal/threshold` for the weight sum, the signature cap and the pre-authorization exclusion instead of restating them, so a rule cannot drift from the semantics 0.7 cited line by line.

Severities are the catalog's where the catalog gives one. Four rows the catalog phrases "by role" shipped at a fixed value with the reason written down, because 3.4 was not open yet, and `sig-single-key-high` needed a decision rather than a guess: it emits INFO, because a fresh account is thresholds 0/0/0 with one weighted key, 0.7's reading is that a tier of 0 requires a match but no weight, and `check` declares no role, so the only Appendix A row that applies is `other`. Task 3.4 (#40) now raises it per role from the declared value.

Two triggers are deliberately narrower than the table reads, and both are recorded rather than quiet: a key appears in exactly one of the three signer comparison rules, with a declared weight of 0 read as an intent to remove, and `sig-threshold-unreachable` emits one finding per account naming every unreachable tier rather than one per tier, because it sits on the non-acceptable list and a per-tier fingerprint would let an operator accept one tier of a broken configuration and read the account as clean. `TestUnreachableTierCannotBeAccepted` asserts that from `policy.Acceptable` rather than from prose.

Fixtures, which was this issue's Done-when: 6 tables in `signers_test.go` and 3 in `thresholds_test.go`, each with the positive and the negative case plus evidence substring checks, one case for the full account that cannot present its 21st signature, and `TestSignerRulesOnACapturedAccount`, which runs the family against `testdata/horizon/7-extra-signer.json` decoded with `encoding/json` rather than through `internal/source`, so the package's no-I/O claim is not what makes the fixture readable. `TestSignerAndThresholdRulesSkipUnreadAccounts` is written so a guard cannot be tested vacuously: each rule is first shown to fire on a readable account, then shown silent for `Missing` and for `Mismatch`. Two narrowing conditions were mutation-checked by removing each one and naming the test that failed.

The suite paid for itself three times: `rules_test.go`'s registry expectation moved from 7 IDs to 16, and `TestIdentityGapsAreFactsNotFindings`, `TestABlankObservedDomainIsNoDomain` and four `internal/run` cases had been built on snapshots with no signers at all, harmless while no rule read them and a genuine HIGH the moment one did. Each now carries a neutral two-key account with the reason in a comment.

Not claimed by this close: golden outputs per Appendix B scenario, which stay 3.6's job (#42), and that any of it has been run against a live account since it landed, which is 4.1's dogfood (#44).
Task 3.1 is ticked on main at c7931d7 (PR #114). Phase 3 moved to 4 of 7 on that merge.

Closed by #115 (merge `c85566c`, 2026-11-04), which ticked `ROADMAP.md` task 3.4.

Both halves of this issue's Done-when are asserted by a run rather than by a table. `policy.roleSeverities` is Appendix A as data and `policy.SeverityFor` reads it as a floor: a role raises a finding to the severity its own row names and never lowers one, which is what makes "a role cannot hide a non-acceptable rule" structural rather than a special case for `acct-missing`, `acct-network-mismatch` and `sig-threshold-unreachable`. `TestSeverityForNeverLowers` walks every cell against every severity so a future row cannot quietly lower one.

Only eight cells move a report today, and the cells that do not are written down anyway because the appendix named them: `sig-single-key-high` on each row that names it above INFO, `flag-drift` and `flag-undeclared-clawback` for `issuer`, `sig-weight-drift` and `thr-drift` for `treasury`.

Ordering is the tested property, not an assumption: `internal/run` calls `applyRoles` between the evaluator and `applyAccepts`, so an acceptance still covers a finding a role raised, on a fingerprint that never contained severity. `TestRoleAdjustmentRunsBeforeAcceptMatching`, `TestRoleAdjustmentLeavesTheFingerprintAlone` and `TestAuditRoleChangesSeverityNotFingerprint` (the last at the CLI, where the two reports differ only in severity and exit code) pin that.

The two prose cells that are not severities became behavior instead of new rules: `policy.ExpectsHomeDomain` gives `id-no-home-domain` its second trigger, so an `issuer` publishing nothing is a WARN with nothing declared, and `policy.AllowsExpectLocked` gates `expect_locked`, so a declared lock reads as intent for an issuer and is stored-and-unread for every other role. Expiry is judged on the UTC date of the run's own instant, the named day being the last day it holds, midnight UTC the cutover, and a value that is not a date reading as expired rather than open; `TestAcceptExpiryIsJudgedInUTC` holds one date against `time.FixedZone` clocks on both sides, where the local day and the UTC day disagree, and it fails both directions if `now.UTC()` is dropped.

Two source documents disagreed and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved silently: `PRD.md` 6.1 writes `flag-undeclared-clawback` as "WARN (HIGH for issuer)" while Appendix A's issuer row speaks of flags generally. The catalog names the rule by ID and the prose cannot be wrong about it, so the cell is HIGH. The same pass gave 6.1's `sig-single-key-high` cell the `distribution` role its Appendix A row always said, and corrected the count of moving cells from seven to eight, which had been wrong in prose since the table was written.

`internal/policy/accept_test.go` was an empty package stub when this started.

Not claimed: that the eight moving cells are the right weights, which is what the three operators in #7 are for; the facts report, 3.7 (#43); and Appendix B golden outputs, 3.6 (#42).
Task 3.4 is ticked on main at c85566c (PR #115). Phase 3 is 5 of 7 and readiness 51 of 78 on that merge.

Closed by PR #119 (merged as 9cfc19c on 2026-11-05), which ticks ROADMAP 4.2: all sixteen rule articles carry a Role weight row, the guides document install, both commands, the four exit codes, the JSON `facts` block and advice per role, and the policy reference documents every key the loader accepts and every acceptance rule it enforces. The dependencies named in the roadmap, 3.7, closed the same morning.

Closed by PR #119 (merged as 9cfc19c on 2026-11-05), which ticks ROADMAP 4.3: `README.md` now quotes the report footer verbatim as `internal/report.Limits` prints it, keeps the explicit "what this does not check" section, adds the install path and replaces the trimmed sample with two whole reports from live testnet runs.

The first run of the matrix is this PR, and it says what the body predicts: `ci / build-test` passed on `ubuntu-latest` (43s), `macos-latest` (1m25s) and `windows-latest` (1m25s), with `ci / go`, `ci / vuln` and `roadmap-check / gate` unchanged and green beside them.

The step timings are the part worth recording, because a green job is not evidence that a test ran. On `windows-latest`: `build` completed at 11:28:14 and `test` at 11:28:44, so 30 seconds of real compilation and execution, the same 30 seconds the Ubuntu leg spent. macOS is 11:28:13 to 11:28:41. The suite ran on all three rather than being skipped or timing out.

That matters for one claim specifically. The body says the `windows-latest` leg would have rewritten 38 goldens and 12 fixtures into CRLF and reported the whole catalog as failing without `.gitattributes`. It did not, and the only thing between this commit and that outcome is the new file, so the pin holds on a real Windows runner rather than only in theory. The `GOOS=windows` cross-build from a Linux tree could not have proved that.

4.4 stays unticked: the Done-when asks for green on all three on `main`, and this is a pull_request event. The merge is yours, and the tick follows the push run.

# Drips Wave

**Automate open-source contribution cycles and rewards.**

Drips Wave is a platform designed to bridge the gap between open-source funding and daily maintenance work. This app integrates with your repository to run structured, short-term contribution cycles ("Waves") that accelerate development and reward contributors.

This GitHub App enables **Repo Maintainers** to sync their open-source repos to Drips Wave and **apply them to Wave Programs**. 

> [!NOTE]
> It's not necessary to install this app if you're only looking to contribute to issues on Drips Wave.

Head to https://drips.network/wave and open the Maintainer -> Issues tab to get started as a Maintainer on Drips Wave.

Drips Wave is a platform designed to bridge the gap between open-source funding and daily maintenance work. This app integrates with your repository to run structured, short-term contribution cycles ("Waves") that accelerate development and reward contributors.

This GitHub App enables **Repo Maintainers** to sync their open-source repos to Drips Wave and **apply them to Wave Programs**. 

> [!NOTE]
> It's not necessary to install this app if you're only looking to contribute to issues on Drips Wave.

Head to https://drips.network/wave and open the Maintainer -> Issues tab to get started as a Maintainer on Drips Wave.
